chunks: Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan, from Bakr ibn Salih, from al-Hasan ibn Sa'id, from Abdallah ibn al-Mughira, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, who said:

I heard Yunus ibn Zabyan saying: I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and said to him: Hisham ibn al-Hakam is making a grave statement — though I shall summarize some of it for you. He alleges that God is a body, because things are of two kinds: a body, and the action of a body. Therefore it is impermissible that the Maker could be [understood] in the sense of an action, and it is permissible that He could be [understood] in the sense of an actor.

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Woe to him! Does he not know that a body is limited and finite, and an image is limited and finite? So when it admits of limitation, it admits of increase and decrease. And when it admits of increase and decrease, it would be a creation.

He said: I asked, 'So what should I say?' He said: 'Neither a body nor an image. He is the One who gives body to bodies and form to forms. He cannot be divided, cannot have an end-point, cannot increase, and cannot decrease. Had it been as they say, there would be no difference between the Creator and the created, nor between the Originator and the originated. But He is the Originator — there is a difference between the One who gave it a body, gave it a form, and originated it. For nothing resembles Him, nor does He resemble anything.'

key_terms.التنزيه: Tanzih — the doctrine of divine transcendence, affirming that God is entirely unlike His creation
key_terms.جسم: Body/corporeality — a physical, extended, limited entity. The hadith's central argument is that a body, by definition, is finite and thus potentially created.
key_terms.صورة: Image/form — the visible shape or outward appearance of a thing. Like the body, it is limited and finite.
key_terms.مجسم الأجسام: The One who gives body to bodies — God as the source and bestower of corporeality upon material entities, without Himself being corporeal.
key_terms.مصور الصور: The One who gives form to forms — God as the source of all imagery and forms, without Himself being an image.
key_terms.منشئ: Originator/Initiator — the one who brings something into existence from nothing; used to emphasize God's absolute creative power.

ai.seo_question: Does the Quran or hadith say God has a body? What did Imam Sadiq teach about God's transcendence?
ai.summary: In this hadith, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) refutes the anthropomorphist claim attributed to Hisham ibn al-Hakam that God is a body. The Imam argues that corporeality implies limitation, and limitation implies the capacity for increase and decrease, which is a characteristic of created things — thus anything that is a body must be a creature, not the Creator. This is a key text in early Shia kalam (theological discourse) establishing transcendence (tanzih) as foundational: God is neither a body nor an image, but rather the very source and originator of all bodies and forms, entirely unlike His creation.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Abu Abdullah, from Muhammad Bin Ismail, from Al Husayn Bin Al Hassan, from Bakr Bin Salih, from Al Hassan Bin Saeed, from Abdullah Bin Al Mugheira, from Muhammad Bin Ziyad who said,

‘I heard Yunus Bin Zabyan saying, ‘I went over to Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> and said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Hisham Bin Al-Hakam is saying grievous words. Indeed, I shall summarise some from it. He is alleging that Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is a body, because the things are two things, body and deed of the body. Thus, it is not permissible that the Maker could happen to be in the meaning of the deed, and it is permissible that He<sup>azwj</sup> could happen to the in the meaning of the performer’.

So Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Weo be unto him! Does he not know that the body is limited to its end-points, and the image is limited to its end-points? So when it carries the limitation, it would carry the increase and the decrease. And when it carries the increase and the decrease, it would be a creation’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘I said, ‘So what should I be saying?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Neither a body, nor an image, and He<sup>azwj</sup> is the Sculptor of the bodies and the Artist of the images. He<sup>azwj</sup> cannot be divided, and cannot have boundaries, and cannot be increased, and cannot be decreased. Had it been as they are saying, there would not be any difference between the Creator and the created, nor between the Constructor and the constructed. But He<sup>azwj</sup> is the Constructor. There is a difference between the One<sup>azwj</sup> Who Sculpts it and Images it and Constructs it, when it was so than there is nothing resembling Him<sup>azwj</sup>, nor does He<sup>azwj</sup> resemble anything’.
en.sarwar: 6. Muhammad ibn Abu ‘Abdallah has narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma‘il from al-Husayn ibn al-Hassan from Bakr ibn Salih from al-Hassan ibn Sa‘id from ‘Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah from Muhammad ibn Ziyad who has said the following.

“I heard Yunus ibn Zabyan saying, ‘I went to meet abu ‘Abdallah (a.s.), and said, “Hisham ibn al-Hakam has uttered monstrous words. I will briefly mention a few words. He thinks Allah has a body because things are of two types; (a) body and (b) the acts. It is not possible for the Creator Himself to be just actions or functions. But it is possible to consider Him as the agent.”

Abu ‘Abdallah (a.s.) then said, ‘That is not proper from him. Does he not know that the body has limits and the form has limits and an end? Whatever is subject to limitations is also subject to increase and reduction and such things are created.’

I then asked, “What then I should say?” He replied, ‘Allah is without body and form. He is the giver of body to all bodies and the giver of form to all forms. He can not be divided or limited. He does not grow or decrease. If it were as they say, then there would have been no difference between the Creator and the created, the inventor and the invented. But He is the Creator and the inventor. He has made the distinction and differentiation between that to which He has given body, form and that which He has invented. This is because nothing is similar to Him nor He resembles anything.’”
